title: Out and About
description: Getting things done and dealing with people: paying, sending and returning things, travel bookings, favours, and arranging to meet. A few are casual, for friends.

items.indonesian: Kalau macet, kita naik ojek saja.
items.english: If the traffic's bad, let's just take an ojek.
items.registerNotes: Saja after a choice means 'just, simply'. Kalau needs no 'it is': kalau macet, if (it's) jammed.
items.cultureNote: An ojek is a motorbike taxi, usually booked on an app. It can slip through traffic that cars can't.

items.indonesian: Tadi saya sudah bayar di kasir.
items.english: I already paid at the till earlier.
items.registerNotes: Tadi is 'earlier today', and it often comes with sudah. Useful when you're asked to pay a second time.

items.indonesian: Ini bisa tolong dibungkus?
items.english: Could you wrap this up for me?
items.registerNotes: Bisa tolong with a di- verb makes a very polite request: it names the thing and leaves out who does it. Good for takeaway and leftovers.
items.pitfallNote: Dibungkus is one word: di- joined to a verb is the passive, unlike di (at) before a place.

items.indonesian: Maaf, bajunya kebesaran. Bisa tukar yang lebih kecil?
items.english: Sorry, the top's too big. Could I swap it for a smaller one?
items.pitfallNote: Kebesaran is the spoken 'too big': ke-…-an around a describing word. Kekecilan is too small.

items.indonesian: Kalau beli dua, ada diskon?
items.english: Is there a discount if I buy two?
items.registerNotes: Kalau puts the condition first. Offering to buy more is a polite way to ask for a better price.

items.indonesian: Kita tawar dulu, jangan langsung bayar.
items.english: Let's bargain first; don't pay straight away.
items.registerNotes: Said to a companion at a market. Dulu here means 'first', before doing anything else, and tawar is menawar without the me-.

items.indonesian: Bisa bayar tunai, atau harus transfer?
items.english: Can I pay cash, or does it have to be a transfer?
items.cultureNote: Bank transfers and QR payments are common everywhere from homestays to market stalls, so it's worth asking before you count on cash.

items.indonesian: Saya sudah transfer, ini buktinya.
items.english: I've made the transfer. Here's the proof.
items.cultureNote: Sending a screenshot of the transfer, the bukti transfer, is the normal way to show you've paid.

items.indonesian: Ongkirnya berapa kalau dikirim ke Bandung?
items.english: How much is delivery if it's sent to Bandung?
items.registerNotes: Ongkir is short for ongkos kirim, the delivery charge. Dikirim is the di- form of kirim (send): 'is sent'.

items.indonesian: Paketnya sudah sampai, tapi isinya rusak.
items.english: The parcel's arrived, but what was inside is broken.
items.registerNotes: Isinya is 'its contents', from isi. Rusak covers broken, damaged and out of order.

items.indonesian: Mbak, saya mau isi pulsa lima puluh ribu.
items.english: I'd like fifty thousand of phone credit, please.
items.registerNotes: Isi pulsa is topping up your phone. Mbak is a polite way to address a young woman serving you, and Mas a young man.
items.cultureNote: You can top up at any minimarket or phone-credit stall, or in a banking app.

items.indonesian: Bisa tolong jemput saya di bandara jam tujuh malam?
items.english: Could you pick me up at the airport at seven in the evening?
items.registerNotes: In requests the me- often drops: jemput rather than menjemput, still polite after bisa tolong. Malam after the hour makes it p.m.

items.indonesian: Kapal ke Gili berangkat jam berapa?
items.english: What time does the boat to Gili leave?
items.pitfallNote: Use berangkat, not pergi, for a boat, bus or plane leaving at a set time.

items.indonesian: Tiketnya sudah habis untuk hari ini.
items.english: Tickets for today are sold out.
items.registerNotes: Habis (used up, all gone) is how 'sold out' is said. It's also what you'll hear when a dish has run out: Maaf, sudah habis.

items.indonesian: Sewa motornya berapa sehari?
items.english: How much is it to hire a scooter for a day?
items.registerNotes: Sehari is 'a day, per day', with se- for one. Seminggu works the same way for a week.

items.indonesian: Kami cari penginapan yang dekat pantai dan tidak terlalu mahal.
items.english: We're looking for somewhere to stay near the beach that isn't too expensive.
items.registerNotes: Yang joins a description to a noun: penginapan yang dekat pantai, somewhere to stay that is near the beach.

items.indonesian: Kalau malam, daerah ini aman?
items.english: Is this area safe at night?
items.registerNotes: Kalau malam is 'at night', in the sense of whenever it's night. Your host or the hotel staff are the best people to ask.

items.indonesian: Koper saya ketinggalan di taksi.
items.english: I left my suitcase in the taxi.
items.pitfallNote: Ketinggalan is 'left behind by accident': the ke-…-an form says it happened to you rather than that you did it.

items.indonesian: Tolong hubungi saya kalau ada kabar.
items.english: Please get in touch if there's any news.
items.registerNotes: Hubungi is menghubungi with the me- dropped, as often in requests. Kabar (news) is the same word as in Apa kabar?

items.indonesian: Boleh pinjam pulpennya sebentar?
items.english: Could I borrow your pen for a moment?
items.registerNotes: Pulpennya, 'the pen', politely stands in for 'your pen' without having to say 'you'. Boleh asks permission: may I.

items.indonesian: Bisa tolong fotokan kami?
items.english: Could you take a photo of us?
items.registerNotes: Fotokan is foto with -kan: take a photo for someone. Kami, not kita, because the person taking it isn't in the photo.

items.indonesian: Maaf, saya tidak sengaja.
items.english: Sorry, I didn't mean to.
items.registerNotes: For bumping into someone or knocking something over. Sengaja is 'on purpose'.

items.indonesian: Antreannya panjang sekali, kita datang lagi nanti saja.
items.english: The queue's really long. Let's come back later.
items.registerNotes: Datang lagi is 'come again, come back'. Nanti saja (just later) is a soft way to put something off.

items.indonesian: Nanti malam kita nongkrong di kafe dekat kosku, yuk.
items.english: Let's hang out at the café near my place tonight.
items.registerNotes: Casual, between friends. Yuk on the end makes it 'let's'. A kos is a rented room in a boarding house, home to many students and young workers.

items.indonesian: Aku udah di depan, kamu di mana?
items.english: I'm out the front. Where are you?
items.registerNotes: Casual: udah is the spoken sudah. Di depan, 'at the front', usually means outside the building or at the gate.
